title: Emergency funds

objectives.text: Explain what an emergency fund is for and what it is not for.
Estimate a suitable size for your own emergency fund.
Choose where to keep an emergency fund so it is safe and reachable.

explanation: An emergency fund is money kept aside for events you cannot plan: a sudden medical bill, a job loss, an urgent trip home, or a major repair. It is not a holiday fund or a down payment. Its job is to stop an emergency from becoming a loan at a high interest rate.

A common rule of thumb is three to six months of essential expenses. This is widely used guidance, not a regulatory requirement, so treat any figure as a starting point that depends on how stable your income is. A salaried household with two earners may need less; a single freelancer may want more.

Keep the fund somewhere safe and quick to reach. A separate savings account or a short-term deposit works for most people. Avoid equity, long lock-ins or anything whose value can fall just when you need the money. Rebuild the fund after using it.

examples.title: Sizing the fund
examples.text: Priya's essential monthly expenses are ₹22,000: rent, food, transport, medicines and the loan instalment. Three months of essentials is ₹66,000 and six months is ₹1,32,000. She targets ₹66,000 first and adds more while her job situation is uncertain.

examples.title: Using it, then rebuilding
examples.text: Rahul's father needs an unplanned procedure costing ₹40,000. He pays from the emergency fund instead of a credit card, then restores the balance over the next five months by redirecting his monthly savings.

keyTakeaways: An emergency fund covers unplanned essentials, not planned wants.
Three to six months of essential expenses is a starting point, not an RBI rule.
Keep it safe and reachable: a separate account or short-term deposit.
After using it, rebuild it before resuming other goals.

review.notes: The save-before-spend and accessible-savings principles are checked against RBI FAME 4th edition, Message 1. The three-to-six-month range is labelled as common guidance, not a regulatory rule; no source is cited for that figure because it is a rule of thumb. Awaiting a named human reviewer.

quiz.question: Which of these is a genuine use of an emergency fund?
options: A festival sale you did not want to miss
quiz.explanation: Emergency funds exist for unplanned essentials. A sale or a planned holiday should come from separate savings.

quiz.question: How should you size your emergency fund?
options: Always exactly six months, whatever your situation
From your essential expenses and how stable your income is
quiz.explanation: Essentials determine what you must cover. Stability of income decides whether you sit at the lower or higher end of the common three-to-six-month range.

quiz.question: Where is the most suitable place for an emergency fund?
options: A separate savings account or short-term deposit
quiz.explanation: The fund must be safe and quickly available. Volatile or locked products can lose value or trap the money exactly when it is needed.

disclaimer: General financial education, not personalised advice. Choose a fund size that reflects your own obligations and income stability.
